opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so if you just count robot arms, you get a pretty big number, because there are a lot of industrial robots out there. But the vast majority of them are doing something very different from what you'd want for training a general-purpose robotic foundation model. An industrial arm in a car factory is typically executing a pre-programmed trajectory over and over again, the same weld, the same pick, in a highly controlled environment. There's no perception in the loop in a meaningful sense, there's no variability, and frankly there's often no logging infrastructure that records the kind of data you'd need: camera observations, the actions, the context of the task.

So even though those machines are physically robot arms, the data they produce is almost worthless for learning. Repeating the same motion a million times doesn't teach you anything new after the first few times. What you actually want is diverse data: different objects, different environments, different tasks, ideally with some failures and recoveries in there too, because that's what lets a model generalize.

The other piece is the form factor and the setup. A lot of those arms are bolted into cells behind safety cages, they're huge, they're not designed to work around people, and they're not instrumented with the kinds of sensors we'd use. So the number of arms that are actually in a configuration where they could be collecting useful, varied, sensorized data is a tiny fraction of the total.

I think the more meaningful question is: how many robots are deployed in a way where they're doing varied, open-world tasks and their experience can be captured and fed back into training? That number is much smaller today. But the encouraging thing is that once you have models good enough to be genuinely useful, you get a flywheel. Robots get deployed because they're useful, the deployment generates diverse data, and that data makes the models better. So in some sense the count that matters isn't how many arms exist, it's how many are participating in that loop.

r001.rationale: The response says industrial arms in car factories repeat preprogrammed tasks in controlled settings and that their data is almost worthless for training a general-purpose model.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the thing is, if you just go and count up all the robot arms that exist in the world, you get a very large number. There are millions of industrial arms out there in factories, doing welding, doing painting, moving parts around on assembly lines. But the vast majority of those are not really useful for what we want to do in terms of training large robotic foundation models, and there are a few reasons for that.

The first is that a lot of those arms are essentially running fixed programs. They're doing the same motion over and over again in a highly structured environment. So even if you could log all of that data, it's not very interesting data. It's not diverse, it doesn't involve perception in any meaningful way, it doesn't involve the kind of decision making that we actually want a learned model to acquire. You'd basically be getting millions of examples of the same trajectory.

The second thing is that many of those arms don't have the sensing that you need. If a robot is doing a task blind, with no cameras, just position control, then there's no observation stream to learn from. And a lot of industrial deployments are like that because the environment has been engineered so that the robot doesn't need to look at anything.

And then the third issue, which I think people underestimate, is just access. Even when the data might be useful, it's sitting inside some company's factory, it's proprietary, it's not instrumented for collection, and nobody is going to set up the infrastructure to pipe it out for research purposes. So there's a big gap between the arms that exist and the arms that are actually generating data that you can get your hands on and that would teach a model something.

So the more honest way to think about it is to ask, how many robots are out there that are operating in somewhat unstructured settings, that have cameras or other rich sensors, and where someone is actually in a position to collect and use that data. And when you ask it that way, the number is much, much smaller. It's not millions, it's probably in the thousands, and a good chunk of those are in research labs or in a handful of companies that are specifically trying to do this. That's a very different picture than the headline number suggests, and I think it's the picture that actually matters for figuring out where the data is going to come from.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes factory arms doing repetitive, fixed motions on assembly lines and says most are not useful for training the desired models, which conveys that car-assembly arms are the wrong kind to train on.

astra-6.text:
Well, it depends on what you mean by suitable for training. A lot of robot arms are sitting in factories, doing the same motion over and over again. If you collect a million hours of a robot repeating one motion, that’s very different from a million hours of robots doing a wide variety of tasks. The diversity of the experience matters a lot.

There’s also a difference between an arm that exists and an arm that you can actually use to collect data. Can you control it? Does it have the sensors you need? Can you change what it’s doing? Somebody probably bought that robot to do a particular job, and they might not want you interrupting production to try out your learning algorithm.

So I’d want to know how many robots we can get useful, diverse experience from, and how much it costs to get that experience. Just counting the arms doesn’t really tell you that.

r001.rationale: It says many factory arms repeat the same motion and that diverse experience matters, but it does not specifically suggest that car-assembly arms are unsuitable to train on.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, the tricky thing is that a robot arm isn’t necessarily a system you can learn from. It might be sitting in a factory, repeating a particular motion, and it might not have the sensors or the logging that you need to turn that experience into useful training data. You’d want to know what it saw, what actions it took, and what happened as a result.

And then there’s the question of whether you can actually change what it does. If that robot is part of a production line, you can’t just have it try things and make mistakes. So there’s a big difference between the number of arms that are installed and the number that are available to collect useful experience for learning. The latter depends much more on how those systems are instrumented and operated than on the raw count.

r001.rationale: The response explains that factory robot arms may lack the sensing and logging needed for training and cannot safely experiment on a production line, making them unsuitable sources of learning experience.
